props.gloss_en: the mishnah: [a traveller between town and walled city] who is destined to return to his place reads as his place does
Rava: the mishnah's 'destined to return' was taught only of one destined to return on the night of the fourteenth
Rava: but one not destined to return on the night of the fourteenth reads with them

Rava: whence do I say it? from 'therefore the Jews of the unwalled towns, who dwell in the unwalled towns' (Esther 9:19) -- since 'the Jews of the unwalled towns' is written, why write 'who dwell in the unwalled towns'?
Rava: it teaches that one who is in an unwalled town [even] for the day is called a paruz
the stam: it is reasoning -- since a one-day paruz is called paruz, a one-day mukaf is called mukaf
Rava: a villager who went to a town reads with them either way [whether or not he will return]
the stam: what is the reason? this [villager] ought to read like the townsfolk
the stam: and it is the Sages who were lenient with the villages, so that they supply water and food to their brethren in the cities
the stam: that [lenience] holds when he is in his own place; but when he is in a town he must read like the townsfolk
the baraita as cited: a city-man who went to a town reads as his own place either way
(entertained) a city-man -- can that enter your mind? it depends on whether he will return! rather, is it not [to be read]: a villager [who went to a town reads as his place]?
the stam: have you not emended it anyway? teach [instead]: he reads with them
